title: Xuanzang at Nalanda
hookLine: after deserts and mountains, the traveler sits down and becomes a student again

lines: NALANDA THROUGH ONE PAIR OF EYES.
cards: What does a person do after crossing deserts and mountain passes to reach the place he set out for? Throw a party? Write home?

Xuanzang became a student again. He reached Nalanda, the great monastery of learning in north India that this path visited earlier this year, and instead of collecting texts and hurrying back, he stayed.
He learned the language. He sat in lectures. He read the same difficult books over and over.
Today, Nalanda through one pair of eyes: a guest from China who made it his school.

teach.b: First, the teacher who was waiting. The head of Nalanda in Xuanzang's day was an old monk named Shilabhadra, deeply honored there, his biography says.
And it tells a striking story: years before, Shilabhadra had been ill and in pain, and in a dream he was told to bear it, because a monk from China would come to learn from him.
When Xuanzang arrived, the story of that dream was told to him. Second, what he came to learn.
Shilabhadra taught the Yogacara, a school whose great subject is the mind: how what we experience is shaped by the mind that experiences it.
Xuanzang had come for one long text of that school in particular, and he heard it taught from beginning to end. Third, life inside the walls.
The biography describes monks discussing and debating from morning until night, rooms given to guests, and food supplied so the students could study.
Xuanzang learned Sanskrit well enough to read, argue and later translate.
Fourth, why it matters. He could have filled his bags and left.

He stayed for years, because some things don't open on a first reading. The Dhammapada, the Buddha's sayings, begins with a line that points the same way: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought."
A line like that is easy to say and slow to understand. Depth can look like this: coming back to the same thing until it gives up what it has.

how: In monastic schools of several Buddhist traditions, students still study a few core texts slowly with a teacher, memorizing, discussing and debating them.

practice: Say today's line once, silently: all that we are is the result of what we have thought.
Then rest with just the first half, all that we are, then with the second, and when a thought passes through, ask gently what it's making of this moment. When the mind drifts, come back to the line.
